questions.question: A compare-and-swap instruction CAS(addr, expected, next) does which of the following atomically?
options: Writes next to addr and returns the value that was there before the write
Writes next to addr only if addr currently holds expected, and reports whether it did
Locks addr until the calling thread writes next and releases it explicitly
Swaps the contents of addr and expected so both threads see each other's value
questions.explanation: CAS is a conditional store: the write happens only when the word still equals the value the caller read earlier, and the boolean result tells the caller whether it won. Option 0 describes an unconditional exchange (getAndSet), which cannot detect that another thread intervened.

questions.question: In the ABA trace, thread A read head = N3 and next = N2, then thread B popped N3, popped N2, and pushed a new job that reused node N3. Why does A's CAS(head, N3, N2) succeed?
options: Because the CAS compares the stack's size, which is 2 both before and after B's operations
Because B's push re-linked N2 under N3, restoring the exact structure A observed
Because the CAS compares only the reference held in head, and head is N3 again
Because the JVM's garbage collector reused N3's memory address for the new node
questions.explanation: The CAS asks one question: is head still the reference I read? Node reuse makes the answer yes even though two pops and a push happened. N2 is in the free list, not under N3, so option 1 is false; the GC is not involved because the pool, not the collector, recycled N3.

questions.question: The first TreiberStack in the lesson allocates a fresh Node on every push and never recycles nodes. Why is it immune to ABA on the JVM?
options: Because AtomicReference.compareAndSet internally compares a hidden version number as well
Because a node A still references cannot be collected and reused, so head equal to A's node means nothing changed
Because the JIT compiler reorders the CAS to run before the read of current.next
Because push and pop take an implicit monitor lock on the AtomicReference object
questions.explanation: Garbage collection guarantees a live reference is never recycled, so if head still equals the node A read, no pop of that node has happened in between. AtomicReference has no hidden stamp (that is what AtomicStampedReference adds), and there is no lock anywhere in the structure.

questions.question: In the Michael-Scott queue, an enqueuer finds tail.next is not null. What does it do, and why is this safe?
options: Swings tail forward to tail.next with a CAS and retries; at most one of the competing CASes succeeds
Spins until tail.next becomes null again, because another enqueue is in progress
Appends its node to tail.next.next so that both enqueues are linked in one step
Aborts and returns false, leaving the caller to retry after a backoff
questions.explanation: A non-null tail.next means another thread linked a node but has not yet moved tail. The observer helps by performing that second CAS itself; the original enqueuer's CAS then fails harmlessly because both expected the same old tail. Spinning on another thread's progress would make the queue blocking, not lock-free.

questions.question: A pull request describes a structure as lock-free. Under the formal definition, which statement must be true of it?
options: Every thread finishes each operation within a bounded number of its own steps
No thread ever retries an operation, because each CAS is guaranteed to succeed
The code contains no synchronized blocks, ReentrantLock, or other mutual exclusion
Across all threads, some operation completes within a bounded number of total steps
questions.explanation: Lock-free guarantees system-wide progress: a CAS fails only because another thread's CAS succeeded, so someone always advances. Per-thread bounded completion is the stronger wait-free guarantee. Merely avoiding synchronized is neither necessary nor sufficient; a spin-wait on another thread's flag has no locks and is still blocking.

questions.question: Which production mechanism is the closest analogue of the stamp in AtomicStampedReference?
options: A row-level SELECT ... FOR UPDATE that blocks concurrent writers until commit
A Redis INCRBY that adds to a counter without reading it first
A database sequence that hands out unique identifiers to concurrent inserters
An UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ? that affects zero rows if the row changed
questions.explanation: Optimistic locking stores a version with the row and makes the write conditional on the version the writer read; a zero-row update is a failed CAS, and the writer re-reads. FOR UPDATE is pessimistic locking, the blocking alternative; INCRBY is an unconditional atomic add with no stale-read detection.
